lines: Your car loan payment is 239 dollars a month. But add insurance, gas and upkeep, and the car really costs about 559 dollars a month.
Cars lose value as they age. That's depreciation. A new car often loses about 20 percent in its first year. A 26,000 dollar car can be worth 20,800 a year later.
The sticker price isn't what you pay. Add sales tax, title and registration, and dealer fees. On a 12,000 dollar car, that's 13,070 out the door.
The 20, 4, 10 rule. Put at least 20 percent down. Borrow for no more than 4 years. And keep the payment plus insurance at or under 10 percent of your monthly income before taxes.
On 3,000 dollars a month, 10 percent is 300. The 239 dollar payment plus 150 of insurance is 389, so this car is a stretch. An 8,000 dollar car passes all three tests.
Get preapproved by a bank or credit union before you shop. On 10,000 dollars for 4 years, 7 percent instead of the dealer's 9 saves 450 dollars.
Negotiate the out-the-door price, not the monthly payment. And before buying a used car, pay your own mechanic to inspect it.
Great horned owls move into old nests other birds built. Buying a good used car is the same idea: the first owner already paid for the biggest drop in value.
